name: ANITA

facility_roles.quote: ANITA I launched December 15, 2006, and flew for ~35 days onboard a NASA LDB scientific balloon during the 2006-2007 Austral Summer from McMurdo Base, Antarctica.
facility_roles.note: 'host' here means the balloon-launch site, not a detector location: ANITA takes data at float altitude (~37 km) over the Antarctic ice sheet during flight, using the ice sheet itself as a detection medium/aperture, not the launch facility.

intervals.label: ANITA-LITE
intervals.quote: ANITA-LITE launched December 17, 2003 and flew for ~18.5 days onboard a NASA LDB scientific balloon during the 2003 Austral Summer from McMurdo Base, Antarctica, flying piggyback with the TIGER experiment.
intervals.note: End date derived by adding the stated ~18.5-day flight duration to the launch date; not independently stated as a calendar date by the source.

intervals.label: ANITA-I
intervals.quote: ANITA I launched December 15, 2006, and flew for ~35 days onboard a NASA LDB scientific balloon during the 2006-2007 Austral Summer from McMurdo Base, Antarctica.
intervals.note: End date derived from the stated ~35-day flight duration; not independently stated as a calendar date.

intervals.label: ANITA-II
intervals.quote: ANITA II launched December 21, 2008, from Williams Field, Antarctica.
intervals.note: End date derived from the companion paper's stated 31-day flight duration (28.5 live days).

intervals.label: ANITA-III
intervals.quote: The third flight of ANITA (ANITA-III) was launched in December 2014 and completed a 22-day flight.
intervals.note: Only month precision for the launch date is stated; the official ANITA-III campaign page (fetched) gave only a pre-launch schedule statement, not a confirmed launch date.

intervals.label: ANITA-IV
intervals.quote: The ANtarctic Impulsive Transient Antenna (ANITA) NASA long-duration balloon payload completed its fourth flight in December 2016, after 28 days of flight time.
intervals.note: Only month precision for the launch date is stated; no exact end date is given, only the 28-day flight duration.

intervals.label: programme completed
intervals.quote: PUEO leverages experience from and supersedes the successful Antarctic Impulsive Transient Antenna (ANITA) program.
intervals.note: No source fetched this session states a formal end date for the ANITA programme itself; ANITA-IV (December 2016) was its last flight and its successor PUEO (announced 2021, not owned by this workstream / not in the Wave-3 ID registry) supersedes it, so 'completed' is used with a start just after the final flight.

physics_goals.value: Detect ultra-high-energy cosmic neutrinos using the Antarctic ice sheet as a giant radio-detection medium, viewed from a balloon-borne antenna array
physics_goals.quote: ANITA observes the Antarctic ice sheet out to a horizon approaching 700 km, giving a neutrino detection volume of near one million cubic kilometers.

unique_capabilities.value: A balloon-borne radio antenna array flown at high altitude over Antarctica, giving an enormous neutrino detection volume without any fixed in-ice or undersea infrastructure
unique_capabilities.quote: Flying at 120,000ft (~37 km), the instrument observes ~1.5 million square kilometers of ice.

ANITA's successor, PUEO (Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations), is named in a Washington University in St. Louis news page as superseding ANITA; PUEO is not modelled here (not an id this workstream owns per the Wave-3 ID registry, and not itself in the astro-neutrino coverage file).

The famous 'ANITA anomalous events' (steeply upward-going radio pulses inconsistent with standard-model neutrino propagation, reported around 2016-2020) are not recorded as a result in this pass; results are an optional extra for non-flagship experiments and were deprioritised in favour of completing the mandatory record set for all nine experiments in this coverage file.

summary.plain: A radio antenna array flown high over Antarctica on a NASA balloon, using the entire ice sheet below as a giant listening surface for ultra-high-energy neutrinos and cosmic rays. It flew five times between 2003 and 2016.
summary.technical: Balloon-borne radio-Cherenkov (Askaryan effect) UHE neutrino/cosmic-ray detector flown at ~37 km altitude over Antarctica, launched from the NASA long-duration-balloon facility near McMurdo Station. Five flights: ANITA-LITE (2003), ANITA-I (2006-2007), ANITA-II (2008-2009), ANITA-III (2014-2015) and ANITA-IV (2016-2017); superseded by the PUEO mission.
